title: Mini Project
overview: You've learned every core concept of Python. Now it's time to use all of them together. In this final lecture, you'll build three complete, real-world Python projects that bring together variables, loops, conditionals, functions, data structures, and file handling.

sections.label: What You've Built — What Comes Next

blocks.content: Over the past 13 lectures, you've built an incredible foundation. Let's take a moment to see just how much you know.

You can store data with **variables** and choose the right container — lists, tuples, sets, dictionaries.

You can make decisions with **conditionals** and repeat actions with **for** and **while loops**.

You can write reusable logic with **functions**, manipulate **strings**, and persist data with **file handling**.
A real Python program combines all of these. The mini project is your chance to do exactly that.

analogy.title: Building a House
analogy.description: You've learned all the tools: hammer (variables), saw (loops), blueprint reading (conditionals), wiring (functions), plumbing (file I/O), and materials (data structures). The mini project is you actually building the house.
bullets: You don't build a house in one attempt — you plan and follow a blueprint.
Foundation first, then walls, then roof — each stage builds on the last.
Every skill you learned in construction comes together in the final build.
analogy.highlightCard: A project brings all your individual Python skills together into one working program.

visualization.title: Skills You're Using
bullets: Variables and data types store all your program's information.
Functions organize logic into reusable, testable building blocks.
Loops, conditions, and data structures control flow and manage collections.
visualization.highlightCard: Every Python concept you've learned is a tool — projects are where you use them all together.

blocks.content: Build a complete student grade management system. The program should allow you to add students, view all students, calculate averages, and save the data to a file.

**Features to implement:**
- Add a student with their name and marks
- View all students and their average marks
- Find the top scorer
- Save all records to a file
- Load records from the file on startup

blocks.title: Try It — Student Grade Manager
blocks.code:
import os

# Data storage
students = {}
FILE = "grades.txt"

def load_data():
    if os.path.exists(FILE):
        with open(FILE, "r") as f:
            for line in f:
                name, marks = line.strip().split(":")
                students[name] = [int(m) for m in marks.split(",")]

def save_data():
    with open(FILE, "w") as f:
        for name, marks in students.items():
            f.write(f"{name}:{','.join(map(str, marks))}\n")

def add_student(name, marks):
    students[name] = marks
    save_data()
    print(f"Added: {name}")

def view_all():
    if not students:
        print("No students yet.")
        return
    print(f"\n{'Name':<15} {'Average':>8} {'Grade':>6}")
    print("-" * 32)
    for name, marks in students.items():
        avg = sum(marks) / len(marks)
        grade = "A" if avg >= 90 else "B" if avg >= 75 else "C" if avg >= 60 else "F"
        print(f"{name:<15} {avg:>8.1f} {grade:>6}")

def top_student():
    if not students:
        return
    best = max(students, key=lambda n: sum(students[n])/len(students[n]))
    avg = sum(students[best]) / len(students[best])
    print(f"Top student: {best} ({avg:.1f})")

# Demo
load_data()
add_student("Priya", [92, 88, 95, 90])
add_student("Arjun", [75, 82, 79, 88])
add_student("Meera", [98, 95, 97, 99])

view_all()
top_student()
blocks.expectedOutput:
Added: Priya
Added: Arjun
Added: Meera

Name            Average  Grade
--------------------------------
Priya              91.2      A
Arjun              81.0      B
Meera              97.2      A
Top student: Meera (97.2)

analogy.title: School Register
analogy.description: A school's grade register has student names (dictionary keys), their marks (list values), computes averages, identifies top performers, and archives records (file handling). Your program automates exactly this manual process.
bullets: The register stores each student's name, grades, and attendance.
The teacher can add new students, update grades, and search by name.
At any time, the teacher can print the full class report.
analogy.highlightCard: A grade manager is a real project — it stores, retrieves, and displays student data.

visualization.title: Grade Manager Architecture
bullets: A dictionary maps each student name to their list of grades.
Functions handle adding students, recording grades, and calculating averages.
A loop displays the full report by iterating over every student.
visualization.highlightCard: Student name → grades dictionary + functions + loops = a complete grade manager.

highlights: grades = {} creates an empty dictionary to store all student data.
grades[name] = [] adds a new student with an empty grade list.
sum(grades[name]) / len(grades[name]) calculates the average grade.
code.highlightCard: Dictionaries, functions, and loops — three Python tools that build every real program.

reflection.question: Which data structure is most suitable for the student-marks relationship?
reflection.answer: Dictionary with student name as key and a list of marks as value — it maps each name to their associated data directly.
options: A dictionary with name as key and list of marks as value

blocks.content: Build an interactive quiz game with multiple questions, score tracking, and a final result. The game asks questions one by one, accepts answers, gives immediate feedback, and shows a final score.

blocks.title: Try It — Quiz Game
blocks.code:
def run_quiz(questions):
    score = 0
    total = len(questions)
    
    print("=" * 40)
    print("    PYTHON 2.0 QUIZ CHALLENGE")
    print("=" * 40)
    print()
    
    for i, q in enumerate(questions, 1):
        print(f"Q{i}: {q['question']}")
        for j, option in enumerate(q['options'], 1):
            print(f"  {j}. {option}")
        
        # Simulate answer (in real app, use input())
        user_answer = q['correct']  # Auto-correct for demo
        
        if user_answer == q['correct']:
            score += 1
            print("  ✓ Correct!")
        else:
            print(f"  ✗ Wrong. Answer: {q['correct']}")
        print()
    
    # Final result
    percent = (score / total) * 100
    print("=" * 40)
    print(f"Score: {score}/{total} ({percent:.0f}%)")
    
    if percent >= 80:
        print("Excellent! You're a Python pro!")
    elif percent >= 60:
        print("Good job! Keep practising.")
    else:
        print("Keep learning — you'll get there!")

# Quiz data
quiz_questions = [
    {"question": "What does len() return?", 
     "options": ["The type", "The length", "The sum", "The first item"],
     "correct": "The length"},
    {"question": "Which creates a list?",
     "options": ["(1,2,3)", "{1,2,3}", "[1,2,3]", "{1:2}"],
     "correct": "[1,2,3]"},
    {"question": "What does 7 % 3 equal?",
     "options": ["2", "3", "1", "4"],
     "correct": "1"}
]

run_quiz(quiz_questions)
blocks.expectedOutput:
========================================

========================================

  2. The length

analogy.title: Game Show
analogy.description: A game show host reads questions, a contestant answers, the host reveals if it's correct, the score accumulates, and at the end a final verdict is given. Your quiz game is a digital game show — same structure, all in Python.
bullets: The host reads a question and the contestant has a fixed time to answer.
Right answer: points are added. Wrong answer: move to the next question.
After all questions, the host announces the final score.
analogy.highlightCard: A quiz program follows the same flow: ask, validate, score, and report.

visualization.title: Quiz Architecture
bullets: A list of question dictionaries stores the quiz content.
A loop iterates through questions, collecting and checking each answer.
A score variable accumulates the total and is displayed at the end.
visualization.highlightCard: Question list + answer loop + score accumulator = a complete Python quiz program.

highlights: questions = [{'q': ..., 'a': ...}, ...] stores the full question bank.
The for loop iterates through every question automatically.
score += 1 adds a point each time the user's answer matches the correct one.
code.highlightCard: A quiz program demonstrates every Python concept in action — from lists to loops to conditionals.

reflection.question: Why store questions as a list of dictionaries instead of separate variables?
reflection.answer: It lets you loop through all questions uniformly, add new questions without changing the code, and access question/answer fields by name.
options: It lets you loop uniformly and add questions without changing code

blocks.stage2Transition: Here is how the quiz program is structured in Python.
blocks.takeaway: A game show quiz is a complete Python program — questions in a list, answers in a loop, score accumulated and displayed at the end. This is what real Python programs look like.

blocks.title: Add a Timer
blocks.instructions:
Enhance the quiz: add an import time, and at the end of run_quiz, calculate how long the quiz took (from start time to end time). Print 'Time taken: X seconds' in the final result.

Hint: Use time.time() before and after the questions loop.
blocks.starterCode:
import time

def run_quiz_timed(questions):
    start = time.time()
    score = 0
    
    for q in questions:
        print(q["question"])
        # Simulate answer
        score += 1
    
    end = time.time()
    elapsed = round(end - start, 2)
    
    print(f"Score: {score}/{len(questions)}")
    print(f"Time taken: {elapsed} seconds")

questions = [
    {"question": "What is len([1,2,3])?"},
    {"question": "What is 7 % 3?"}
]

run_quiz_timed(questions)
blocks.hint: Save time.time() before the loop as start. Save it again after as end. elapsed = end - start.
blocks.expectedOutput:
What is len([1,2,3])?
What is 7 % 3?
Score: 2/2
Time taken: 0.0 seconds

keyTakeaways.text: Real programs combine all Python concepts: variables, loops, conditionals, functions, data structures, and file I/O.
Dictionaries are ideal for structured data where each record has named fields.
Functions keep your code organised — each function has one clear responsibility.
File handling makes your programs persistent — data survives after the program ends.
The accumulator pattern appears in every project: initialise, update in loop, use after.
Good program design: write small functions, combine them, test each separately.

whatYouLearned: How to combine all Python concepts into a working program
How to design a Student Grade Manager with persistence
How to build an interactive quiz game
Principles of program design: small functions, clear data structures, file-backed storage

quiz.question: In a student grade manager using a dictionary, what should be the key and value?
options: Key: student name, Value: marks list
Key: grade, Value: all students with that grade
quiz.answer: Key: student name, Value: marks list
quiz.explanation: Dictionary keys should be the unique identifier (name) and values should be the associated data (marks list). This allows direct lookup by name: students['Priya'] → [92, 88, 95].

quiz.question: Why should a program have a save_data() function that's called after every change?
options: To ensure changes persist even if the program crashes
To prevent the dictionary from growing too large
quiz.answer: To ensure changes persist even if the program crashes
quiz.explanation: In-memory data (dictionaries, lists) is lost when the program ends or crashes. Saving to a file immediately after each change ensures no data is lost.

quiz.question: What is the best data structure to store quiz questions with question text, options, and correct answer?
quiz.explanation: Each question is a dictionary with named fields (question, options, answer). A list of such dictionaries lets you loop through all questions uniformly and access fields by name.

quiz.question: How do you calculate the percentage score in a quiz?
quiz.explanation: Percentage = (correct answers ÷ total questions) × 100. Always multiply by 100 to get the percentage form.

quiz.question: Which of these best describes good function design?
options: One large function that does everything
Many small functions, each with one clear responsibility
quiz.answer: Many small functions, each with one clear responsibility
quiz.explanation: This is the Single Responsibility Principle. Small, focused functions are easier to test, debug, reuse, and understand. The grade manager example shows this: separate functions for add, view, save, load, and top_student.

problems.title: Number Analyser
problems.description:
Write a program that:
1. Asks user for 5 numbers
2. Computes: min, max, sum, average
3. Counts how many are positive, negative, zero
4. Lists the even numbers
5. Prints a formatted report

Simulate with: numbers = [12, -5, 0, 8, -3]
problems.solution:
numbers = [12, -5, 0, 8, -3]

print("=== Number Analysis ===")
print(f"Numbers: {numbers}")
print(f"Min: {min(numbers)}")
print(f"Max: {max(numbers)}")
print(f"Sum: {sum(numbers)}")
print(f"Average: {sum(numbers)/len(numbers)}")

pos = sum(1 for n in numbers if n > 0)
neg = sum(1 for n in numbers if n < 0)
zero = numbers.count(0)
print(f"Positive: {pos}, Negative: {neg}, Zero: {zero}")

evens = [n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0]
print(f"Even numbers: {evens}")

testCases.label: Number analysis
testCases.expectedOutput:
=== Number Analysis ===
Numbers: [12, -5, 0, 8, -3]
Min: -5
Max: 12
Sum: 12
Average: 2.4
Positive: 2, Negative: 2, Zero: 1
Even numbers: [12, 0, 8]

problems.title: Text Adventure Game
problems.description:
Build a mini text adventure game with these rooms and connections:
- You start in 'Hall'
- Hall connects to: Kitchen (north), Garden (south)
- Kitchen connects to: Hall (south), Pantry (east)
- Garden connects to: Hall (north)
- Pantry: 'You found the treasure! You win!'

Allow the player to move by typing directions. End when they reach Pantry or quit.
problems.starterCode:
rooms = {
    "Hall": {"north": "Kitchen", "south": "Garden"},
    "Kitchen": {"south": "Hall", "east": "Pantry"},
    "Garden": {"north": "Hall"},
    "Pantry": {}
}

current_room = "Hall"

print("=== TEXT ADVENTURE ===")
print("Find the treasure! Type directions to move. Type 'quit' to exit.\n")

# Simulate moves: north, east (to reach Pantry)
moves = ["north", "east"]

for move in moves:
    print(f"You are in: {current_room}")
    exits = list(rooms[current_room].keys())
    print(f"Exits: {', '.join(exits)}")
    print(f"You go {move}...")
    
    if move in rooms[current_room]:
        current_room = rooms[current_room][move]
    else:
        print("You can't go that way!")
    
    if current_room == "Pantry":
        print("You found the treasure! You win!")
        break
    print()

testCases.label: Adventure game
testCases.expectedOutput:
=== TEXT ADVENTURE ===
Find the treasure! Type directions to move. Type 'quit' to exit.

You are in: Hall
Exits: north, south
You go north...

You are in: Kitchen
Exits: south, east
You go east...
You found the treasure! You win!
